The French Revolution. From seventeen eighty-nine to seventeen ninety-nine, a cataclysm destroyed the old feudal and absolutist order in France and reshaped European civilization. Beginning as a financial crisis and popular uprising for constitutional reform, it escalated into radical upheaval: the storming of the Bastille, the abolition of feudalism, the execution of the king, and the Reign of Terror, during which tens of thousands died on the guillotine. Though revolutionary governments fell and Napoleon ultimately seized power, the Revolution's legacy—the ideas of citizenship, human rights, national sovereignty, and secular law—became irreversible and inspired democratic and nationalist movements across Europe and beyond.

France faced bankruptcy and famine. The calling of the Estates-General in seventeen eighty-nine to levy taxes sparked widespread unrest among the common people, the Third Estate, and lower nobility. The storming of the Bastille on July fourteenth, seventeen eighty-nine, a royal prison in Paris, became the Revolution's symbolic moment and is celebrated as France's national day. It signaled that the populace had the power to defy the crown. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen in August seventeen eighty-nine proclaimed universal principles of liberty, equality, and popular sovereignty, rejecting the divine right of kings.

The Reign of Terror from seventeen ninety-three to seventeen ninety-four, led by Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety, executed thousands of perceived enemies of the Revolution, including King Louis the Sixteenth in seventeen ninety-three and Queen Marie-Antoinette in seventeen ninety-three. The Revolution abolished feudalism, serfdom, and corporate privileges. It created a secular civil code and tried, with mixed success, to de-Christianize France through revolutionary cults. Radical factions like the Jacobins under Robespierre and the more moderate Girondins clashed over the pace and aims of reform. Robespierre's Jacobins gained control and purged rivals.

Thermidor in July seventeen ninety-four saw Robespierre's downfall and execution, ending the Terror. The subsequent Directory from seventeen ninety-five to seventeen ninety-nine stabilized the republic but proved weak and unpopular. Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in the Coup of eighteen Brumaire in November seventeen ninety-nine, establishing the Consulate and eventually the Empire. He preserved revolutionary legal reforms while discarding democratic governance.
